subject: biology

items.q: Water is described as the medium for life. What does this mean?
items.correct: Most of the processes of life take place in aqueous solution.
items.misconception: Water is inert packing between the working parts of a cell.
items.why: GCSE and MYP courses describe cytoplasm as a jelly-like substance and cell diagrams show organelles as the labelled, active parts floating in an unlabelled background, so students never see water as something that takes part. The cytoplasm is an aqueous solution, and it is in this solution that most enzyme-catalysed reactions occur and through which substances move. Water is the medium for life, not the packaging around it, which is why the first cells originated in water and why cells still cannot function without it.
items.specStatementText: Life happens in water: cells are aqueous, wherever they live
items.random_wrong: Every substance that a cell uses must be dissolved in water.

items.q: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?
items.correct: The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
items.misconception: Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
items.why: Charges were introduced at GCSE through ionic bonding, where electrons are transferred completely and written as + and −. The δ symbol looks like a variant of those charge signs rather than a signal that the charge is only partial. In a polar covalent bond the electron pair is shared unequally, not transferred. Oxygen gains only a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+), much smaller than the charge of an ion. The attraction between δ+ hydrogen and δ− oxygen on neighbouring molecules is a hydrogen bond, not an ionic bond.
items.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
items.random_wrong: It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.

items.q: During transpiration, water molecules leave the liquid on the surface of a cell wall and enter the air. Which bonds are broken as each molecule leaves?
items.correct: Hydrogen bonds between it and neighbouring molecules
items.misconception: Polar covalent bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen atoms
items.why: Students learn that bonds break when energy is supplied, and particle diagrams of solids, liquids and gases draw each particle as a single sphere, so they do not distinguish the strong bonds inside a molecule from the weak attractions between molecules. Evaporation and dissolving are physical changes. A water molecule that evaporates keeps both of its O–H covalent bonds; what it breaks are the hydrogen bonds to its neighbours. Likewise a glucose molecule that dissolves stays a whole glucose molecule, now hydrogen-bonded to water instead of to other glucose molecules.
items.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen bonds between the oxygen and hydrogens inside it

items.q: Transpiration puts the column of water in a xylem vessel under tension. Why does the column not break as it is pulled upwards?
items.correct: Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules to each other.
items.misconception: Root pressure pushes the column upwards from below.
items.why: Everyday experience of moving water uses pumps and pushing, and GCSE courses say that roots absorb water and it is then 'transported' upwards, without explaining what provides the force. The idea of a liquid being pulled from above is unfamiliar. In a transpiring plant the driving force is the loss of water from the leaves. The water column in the xylem is under tension (a negative pressure) and is pulled upwards; the column does not break because hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules to one another (cohesion). A pushed column would not need cohesion; a pulled column depends on it.
items.specStatementText: Cohesion: water sticks to water
items.random_wrong: Capillary action lifts the water inside the narrow vessel.

items.q: A pond skater rests on a pond. Its legs make small dents in the water surface but do not pass through it. What allows the surface to support the insect?
items.correct: Cohesion between surface molecules makes the surface act like an elastic film.
items.misconception: The insect is less dense than water, so upthrust holds it at the surface.
items.why: 'Floating' is the everyday word for anything that stays on top of water, and students have learned at GCSE that objects float when they are less dense than the liquid. They apply that single rule to an animal that is actually resting on the surface rather than displacing water. A pond skater is denser than water; if its legs are pushed through the surface it sinks. It is supported because the surface molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds and resist being separated, so the surface dents under the legs but does not break. This is surface tension, a consequence of cohesion, and it lets small animals use the water surface as a habitat.
items.specStatementText: Cohesion: water sticks to water
items.random_wrong: Water adheres to the insect's legs and so holds them up on the surface.

items.q: Water rises through the narrow spaces between soil particles, against gravity. Which explanation of this movement is correct?
items.correct: Water adheres to the polar or charged surfaces of the soil particles.
items.misconception: Cohesion between the water and the soil particles draws the water upwards.
items.why: Both words share the ending '-hesion' and are introduced together, and students meet 'cohesion' first as the headline property of water, so it becomes the label for any sticking that water does. Cohesion is water-to-water attraction due to hydrogen bonds between water molecules; it keeps a column of water in xylem continuous under tension and produces surface tension. Adhesion is water-to-other-substance attraction; it is what makes water cling to polar or charged surfaces and drives capillary action in soil and cell walls.
items.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
items.random_wrong: Water adheres to any solid surface, whatever the surface is made of.

items.q: In a leaf, water evaporates from the cellulose cell walls of spongy mesophyll cells. How does adhesion contribute to water transport?
items.correct: It draws water into the cell walls to replace water that evaporates.
items.misconception: It holds water against the waxy cuticle so that less of it evaporates.
items.why: In everyday life water wets almost every surface students handle (glass, paper, cotton, skin), and all of these happen to be polar. Students have no reason to notice that the surfaces share a property until they see water bead on wax. Adhesion depends on attraction between the δ+ and δ− parts of water molecules and charges or partial charges on the surface. Polar or charged surfaces attract water; non-polar surfaces such as wax or oil do not, so water forms droplets on them instead of spreading. That is why the waxy cuticle of a leaf reduces water loss.
items.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
items.random_wrong: It pushes water out of the xylem into the cell walls under root pressure.

items.q: Why do so many different substances dissolve in water?
items.correct: Polar water molecules attract polar and charged solutes.
items.misconception: Water splits every solute into positive and negative ions.
items.why: Dissolving is taught at GCSE almost entirely through salt, with sodium and chloride ions separating and being surrounded by water, so students take ion formation to be what dissolving is. A wide variety of hydrophilic molecules dissolve in water. Glucose has many hydroxyl (–OH) groups that form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so it dissolves without forming any ions. What matters is whether the molecule is polar or charged, not whether it is ionic.
items.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
items.random_wrong: Water breaks the covalent bonds within the solute molecules.

items.q: Which statement about the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids in a cell membrane is correct?
items.correct: Their insolubility in water is what holds the bilayer together as a barrier.
items.misconception: Their insolubility means that they have no function in the membrane.
items.why: Water is emphasized as the medium for life and the solvent for metabolism, and GCSE digestion is taught as turning 'insoluble' molecules into 'soluble' ones that the body can use, so insolubility comes to sound like uselessness. Membranes exist only because phospholipid tails are insoluble and cluster away from water. Some molecules function precisely because they are hydrophobic and insoluble; the solvent properties of water and the insolubility of certain molecules are both essential to a cell.
items.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
items.random_wrong: They are pushed away from water by a repulsive force from water molecules.

items.q: Glucose is carried dissolved in blood plasma and in phloem sap, and it is broken down by enzymes in the aqueous cytoplasm. Which property of glucose makes this possible?
items.correct: Its many hydroxyl (–OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water.
items.misconception: It is a small molecule, and small molecules dissolve readily.
items.why: GCSE digestion is summarised as 'large insoluble molecules are broken down into small soluble molecules', which makes size and solubility sound like the same property. Starch is insoluble and glucose soluble because of how they are structured and how they interact with water, not simply because one is bigger. What decides solubility is polarity: glucose dissolves because its hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, and a small hydrocarbon does not dissolve because it cannot.
items.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
items.random_wrong: It separates into positive and negative ions in water.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes a consequence of the physical properties of water for a ringed seal (Pusa hispida)?
items.correct: Upthrust from the sea water supports most of its body weight.
items.misconception: Because it can sink, the water gives its body no support.
items.why: 'Float or sink' is taught as a yes/no outcome depending on density, so students think of upthrust as something that appears only when an object floats. Upthrust acts on every body immersed in a fluid, whether it floats or sinks; it is the difference between the upthrust and the weight that decides which happens. For a ringed seal the two nearly balance, so the water carries most of its weight and it needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which gets negligible upthrust from air.
items.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
items.random_wrong: It loses heat slowly because water is a poor conductor of heat.

items.q: Thermal conductivity: water 0.60 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, air 0.025 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Specific heat capacity: water 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, air 1000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A ringed seal in sea water at 5 °C and a black-throated loon standing in air at 5 °C have the same body temperature. Other factors being equal, which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: Heat is conducted away from the seal's skin about 24 times faster.
items.misconception: Heat is conducted away from the seal's skin only about 4 times faster.
items.why: Thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity are both 'heat' properties taught in the same lesson, and 'water heats up slowly' and 'water takes heat away quickly' sound contradictory, so students merge the two properties into one. The two properties are separate. Thermal conductivity is how fast heat passes through a substance: water's is high, so heat leaves an animal's skin rapidly. Specific heat capacity is how much energy is needed to change temperature: water's is high, so a body of water changes temperature slowly. Water both conducts heat away fast and holds its own temperature steady.
items.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
items.random_wrong: The seal loses less heat, because water stores much more heat than air.

items.q: A black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) flies through air and dives through water. Which statement about these two fluids is correct?
items.correct: Water is far more viscous than air, so it resists the loon's movement much more.
items.misconception: Air has no viscosity, so the loon meets no resistance when it flies.
items.why: Viscosity is introduced with thick liquids such as syrup and oil, and 'viscous' is used in everyday language to mean 'thick', so a gas that cannot be felt as thick is assumed to have no viscosity. All fluids, gases included, have viscosity. Air's viscosity is low, so it offers little resistance to a flying loon or a walking animal, whereas water's much higher viscosity strongly resists movement, which is why aquatic animals such as the ringed seal benefit from streamlining.
items.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
items.random_wrong: Water conducts heat more slowly than air, so the loon cools less when diving.

items.q: The Moon formed close to Earth and was struck by the same water-bearing asteroids, yet its surface has almost no water today. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Its gravity is too weak to hold water vapour, which escapes to space.
items.misconception: It has no ozone layer to act as a lid that keeps water vapour in.
items.why: Diagrams of the greenhouse effect and the ozone layer draw the atmosphere as a boundary line around the planet, and 'the atmosphere protects us' is repeated so often that students treat it as a physical barrier. The atmosphere is not a lid; gases can escape from the top of it. What holds water on Earth is gravity, which is strong enough to retain water molecules, together with temperatures low enough for water to condense so that most of it lies in the oceans as liquid rather than as vapour that could be lost. The atmosphere itself is retained by the same gravity.
items.specStatementText: Where Earth's water came from, and why it stayed
items.random_wrong: It had no volcanoes to release water made from rock in its interior.

items.q: Where is most of the water on Earth thought to have come from?
items.correct: From water-bearing asteroids that collided with the early Earth
items.misconception: From hydrogen and oxygen gases that reacted in the early atmosphere
items.why: Chemistry lessons show hydrogen burning in oxygen to make water, and GCSE chemistry teaches that volcanoes released the water vapour that condensed to form the early oceans, so students already hold an 'Earth-made' explanation before they meet the extraplanetary hypothesis. The hypothesis studied in the IB course is that Earth's water came from beyond the planet, delivered by asteroids. Volcanic outgassing moved water from inside the early Earth to its surface but does not explain where that water originally came from, and free hydrogen and oxygen were not available in the early atmosphere to react in the amounts needed.
items.specStatementText: Where Earth's water came from, and why it stayed
items.random_wrong: From water formed inside the Earth and released by volcanoes

items.q: Astronomers find a rocky planet orbiting within the Goldilocks zone of its star. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: Liquid water could exist on its surface, so it is worth investigating.
items.misconception: Liquid water and living organisms must both exist on the planet's surface.
items.why: News headlines announce 'Earth-like planet found in habitable zone' as if habitability had been confirmed, and the fairy-tale name suggests that a planet in the zone is 'just right' in every respect. Being in the Goldilocks zone is a necessary condition for surface liquid water, not proof of it: the Moon is in the same zone as Earth yet has no liquid water on its surface. The zone is used to select which planets to search; the presence of water, and then of life, must be established separately.
items.specStatementText: Looking for life means looking for liquid water
items.random_wrong: It orbits at the same distance from its star as Earth does from the Sun.

items.q: Over a clear spring day and night, the air above a lake varies between 2 °C and 18 °C, but the lake water 1 m below the surface stays between 7 °C and 8 °C. Which explanation of the stable water temperature is correct?
items.correct: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a large energy input or loss is needed to change its temperature.
items.misconception: Water stores a large amount of heat, so the lake is warmer than the air above it throughout the day.
items.why: 'Heat capacity' sounds like an amount of heat stored, and 'stores heat' is read as 'is warm', so a substance with a high heat capacity is imagined to be hot rather than slow to change temperature. Specific heat capacity describes how much energy changes temperature, not how warm something is. The sea around a ringed seal can be close to 0 °C; what water's high specific heat capacity provides is stability, so the seal's habitat does not swing in temperature the way air does between day and night. Heat still leaves the seal rapidly because water conducts heat well.
items.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
items.random_wrong: Water has a high thermal conductivity, so heat passes through it too quickly to change its temperature.

items.q: Two water molecules are drawn using the notation for polarity and hydrogen bonding. Which feature of the drawing is correct?
items.correct: A dashed line joins a hydrogen labelled δ+ on one molecule to the oxygen labelled δ− on the other.
items.misconception: A dashed line joins the oxygen to one of the two hydrogens within the same water molecule.
items.why: The name 'hydrogen bond' sounds like 'the bond that hydrogen makes', and the only bonds students have previously named in water are the O–H bonds inside the molecule. Diagrams that show both kinds of bond on one crowded figure add to the confusion. The bonds within a water molecule are polar covalent bonds. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules: the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the δ− oxygen of another. Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than the covalent bonds and are what break when water evaporates.
items.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
items.random_wrong: The oxygen is labelled with a full − and each hydrogen with a full +, because the molecule is made of ions.

items.q: How strong is a hydrogen bond between two water molecules?
items.correct: Weak compared with a covalent bond: in liquid water hydrogen bonds are continually breaking and re-forming, and it is the very large number of them that produces water's properties.
items.misconception: Hydrogen bonds are strong, permanent bonds, comparable to covalent bonds, that lock water molecules together into a rigid structure.
items.why: Textbooks describe the effects of hydrogen bonding, such as cohesion and the high boiling point of water, as 'strong' effects, and students transfer the word to the individual bonds. Diagrams of hydrogen bonding are static, so the bonds look fixed in place. An individual hydrogen bond has only a small fraction of the strength of a covalent bond and lasts only a fraction of a second in liquid water. Water's cohesion, surface tension and thermal properties arise from the huge number of hydrogen bonds present at any moment, not from the strength of any one of them.
items.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can capillary action on its own move water to the top of a tall tree?
items.correct: No. Capillary action moves water short distances through narrow spaces such as soil pores and cell walls; the pull that raises water many metres up xylem comes from tension generated by transpiration.
items.misconception: Capillary action is the mechanism that lifts water all the way up the xylem from the roots to the leaves of a tall tree.
items.why: Capillary rise is demonstrated with narrow glass tubes in which water visibly climbs, and xylem vessels are also described as narrow tubes, so students assume the same effect carries water the whole height of a plant. Capillary action, which depends on adhesion of water to the polar walls of narrow spaces, can raise water only a limited distance. In plants its role is in soil, where it moves water between particles to the roots, and in cell walls, where it draws water in to replace water that evaporates. Long-distance transport up the xylem is by tension created by transpiration, transmitted through the water column by cohesion.
items.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do hydrophobic molecules not dissolve in water?
items.correct: Because they are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds or other attractions with water, so water molecules keep bonding to each other and the non-polar molecules are excluded.
items.misconception: Water actively repels hydrophobic molecules with a repulsive force, pushing them away.
items.why: 'Hydrophobic' literally means 'water-fearing', and everyday descriptions say that oil and water 'repel' each other, so students imagine a force pushing the two apart. There is no repulsion. Water molecules are strongly attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds, and a non-polar molecule offers nothing to attract them, so it is left out of the water structure and non-polar molecules cluster together. The exclusion of hydrophobic tails from water is what holds phospholipid bilayers together.
items.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would ice or water vapour on a planet be as good as liquid water for supporting life?
items.correct: No. Water can act as the medium for life only as a liquid, in which substances dissolve, enzymes catalyse reactions and materials are transported; ice and vapour cannot do this.
items.misconception: Finding water in any form, such as ice at a planet's poles or vapour in its atmosphere, means the planet could support life just as well as if it had liquid water.
items.why: Headlines about 'water found on Mars' or 'on the Moon' rarely say that the water is ice, so students count any discovery of water as a discovery of habitability. The search for extraterrestrial life focuses on liquid water because life's processes occur in aqueous solution. This is why the Goldilocks zone is defined by temperatures that allow water to be liquid, rather than by the presence of water in any state.
items.specStatementText: Looking for life means looking for liquid water
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water still the medium for life in organisms that live on land or fly in the air?
items.correct: Yes. Their cells are aqueous inside: metabolism takes place in the water of the cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water, so water remains the medium for their life processes.
items.misconception: Organisms that live on land or in the air have air rather than water as the medium for their life processes; water is the medium only for aquatic organisms.
items.why: Students confuse an organism's habitat with the medium in which its cellular processes occur, and the story of life 'leaving the water' to colonise land suggests that water was left behind. Life originated in water and has never left it at the cellular level. A land animal or plant carries its water inside; its cells are largely water, and every metabolic reaction still occurs in aqueous solution. Land organisms need adaptations to conserve water precisely because water remains their medium.
items.specStatementText: Life happens in water: cells are aqueous, wherever they live
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does it mean to say that a water molecule is polar?
items.correct: That it has regions of partial charge: a δ− oxygen and δ+ hydrogens, because the shared electrons in the O–H bonds are drawn towards the oxygen.
items.misconception: A polar molecule is one with a magnetic north and south pole, so water molecules attract each other magnetically.
items.why: 'Polar' and 'poles' are met in everyday life through magnets and through the Earth's geographic poles, so the word suggests magnetism before it suggests electric charge. Polarity in chemistry refers to an uneven distribution of electric charge, not to magnetism. The δ+ end of one water molecule is attracted electrically to the δ− end of another, and this attraction is a hydrogen bond.
items.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules

items.q: What makes water rise through the narrow spaces in soil or in a cell wall?
items.correct: Adhesion of water to the polar or charged surfaces of the spaces, combined with cohesion between water molecules; this is capillary action.
items.misconception: Water is drawn up narrow spaces by suction or by air pressure pushing from below, not by any attraction between the water and the surface.
items.why: The everyday experience of drawing liquid up a straw is explained by 'suction', and pupils meet air pressure as the reason liquid rises in a straw, so any rise of water in a narrow space is attributed to a pressure difference. Capillary action needs no pressure from outside. Water molecules are attracted to the polar or charged walls of the narrow space (adhesion) and to each other (cohesion), so water creeps along the surfaces and pulls more water after it. In a non-polar tube the effect does not occur, which shows that the attraction to the surface is what matters.
items.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water at 5 °C colder than air at 5 °C?
items.correct: No. Both are at the same temperature; water feels colder because it conducts heat away from the skin about 25 times faster than air does.
items.misconception: Water at a given temperature is colder than air at the same temperature, because it feels much colder.
items.why: Students judge temperature from sensation, and what the skin senses is the rate of heat loss, not temperature. Swimming in water that feels icy while the air feels mild reinforces the belief. Temperature is the same for both. The difference is thermal conductivity: water carries heat away from an animal's body far faster than air, which is why a ringed seal needs thick blubber in water that is no colder than the air above it.
items.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it

items.q: Is the Goldilocks zone at the same distance from every star?
items.correct: No. The zone lies where a planet's surface temperature could allow liquid water, so its distance depends on how much energy the star emits: closer for a dim star, further out for a bright one.
items.misconception: The Goldilocks zone is a fixed distance from any star, the same as the distance from the Earth to the Sun.
items.why: The idea is usually introduced with the Solar System as the only example, so the Earth–Sun distance becomes the definition of the zone rather than one instance of it. The zone is defined by temperature, not distance. Around a star that emits less energy than the Sun the zone is closer in; around a brighter star it is further out. Astronomers calculate the zone separately for each star before deciding which of its planets are candidates for liquid water.
items.specStatementText: Looking for life means looking for liquid water
